body_markdown:
Your calf muscles do more than help you walk. Discover how the calf muscle pump supports circulation, why it is called the “second heart,” and what research says about cardiovascular health.


Your calves may not be the first muscles you associate with heart health, but they play a surprisingly important role in keeping blood moving around your body.


Every time you walk, climb stairs, flex your ankles or even move your toes, your calf muscles help push blood from your lower legs back towards your heart. This process is known as the **calf muscle pump** , and researchers are increasingly interested in how well it works and what it might tell us about overall health.


The idea is simple. Your heart pumps blood throughout the body, but blood returning from the legs has to travel upwards against gravity. Muscles in the feet, calves and thighs contract and squeeze nearby veins, helping move blood towards the heart. One-way valves inside the veins help prevent the blood from flowing backwards.


Because of this important role, the calf has sometimes been described as a **“second heart.”** The comparison is not meant to suggest that your calf is literally another heart. Instead, it highlights the muscle’s role in supporting circulation.


## Why the calf muscle pump matters


A 2024 study involving researchers at the Mayo Clinic investigated the relationship between calf muscle pump function and long-term health outcomes.


According to the research, people with impaired calf pump function had substantially higher mortality rates during the study period than people whose calf pump function was normal. Over 10 years, the reported mortality risk was approximately **17.5 per cent among people with impaired calf pump function** , compared with **5.9 per cent among those with normal function** .


These findings are important, but they need to be interpreted carefully. An association between poor calf pump function and mortality does not automatically mean that weak or poorly functioning calf muscles directly cause an increased risk of death.


There may be several factors involved, including age, physical activity, underlying cardiovascular disease and general muscle health.


Still, the research raises an interesting question: could improving calf muscle function become one part of a broader approach to maintaining healthy circulation?


## Your calves work against gravity


When blood reaches your legs, gravity makes its journey back to the heart more difficult.


The calf muscle pump provides mechanical assistance. When the calf contracts, it compresses veins and helps propel blood upwards. When the muscle relaxes, the veins can refill before the next contraction.


This is one reason movement is so important.


Walking regularly activates the calf muscles repeatedly, creating a natural pumping action. The same principle applies when you hike, climb stairs, jog, dance or perform exercises that involve repeated ankle movement.


By contrast, sitting still for long periods means the calf pump is being used much less.


Reduced movement can contribute to blood pooling in the lower legs, which may lead to sensations such as heaviness, discomfort or swelling around the ankles.


## The soleus muscle may have another role


One particularly interesting calf muscle is the **soleus** , a deep muscle located towards the back of the lower leg.


The soleus is active during standing and many forms of low-level movement. Research has explored whether activating this muscle while sitting could influence the body's handling of glucose after eating.


One simple movement involves keeping your toes on the floor while repeatedly raising your heels. This engages the calf muscles without requiring you to stand up or perform vigorous exercise.


Research into this type of movement suggests that low-intensity soleus activity may have metabolic benefits, particularly for glucose regulation.


That does not mean seated calf raises are a replacement for regular exercise or medical treatment. Instead, they could potentially be a useful addition to an active lifestyle, especially for people who spend long periods sitting.


## Walking is still one of the simplest options


You do not need complicated equipment to activate your calf muscles.


Walking is one of the easiest ways to keep the calf pump working throughout the day. Hiking, jogging and stair climbing can provide additional challenges, while exercises such as calf raises can specifically target the muscles.


Strength training may also become increasingly important as we get older.


Muscle mass and strength naturally tend to decline with age, and maintaining strong legs can support mobility, balance and independence. Stronger calf muscles may also help maintain the mechanical action involved in returning blood from the lower legs.


However, researchers are still investigating exactly how changes in calf strength and calf pump function translate into long-term health outcomes.


In other words, it is too early to claim that stronger calves will necessarily make you live longer.


## Cardiovascular fitness is not the whole picture


It is easy to think of cardiovascular health primarily in terms of aerobic exercise. Activities such as running, cycling and swimming are excellent ways to challenge the heart and lungs.


But maintaining muscle strength matters too.


A balanced exercise routine can include aerobic activity, resistance training, mobility exercises and balance work. Together, these forms of movement can help you stay physically capable and active throughout life.


An important point is that the benefits of exercise do not come solely from what happens to your heart rate during a workout. Muscles, blood vessels, bones, joints and the nervous system all respond to regular physical activity.


Your calves are part of that larger system.


## What can your calves really tell you about your heart?


At present, your calf muscles should not be considered a standalone test for heart disease.


Changes such as swelling, persistent pain, weakness or unusual differences between your legs can have many possible causes. Some symptoms can require prompt medical assessment, particularly if they develop suddenly or are accompanied by chest pain or breathing difficulties.


The emerging research is better viewed as a reminder of the close relationship between movement, muscle function and circulation.


Your calves are constantly helping your cardiovascular system, often without you noticing.


So the next time you walk up a flight of stairs or take a stroll around the neighbourhood, remember that you are not only exercising your legs. You are also repeatedly activating a natural pumping mechanism that helps return blood towards your heart.


The humble calf muscle may not be a second heart in the literal sense, but its contribution to circulation is certainly worth paying attention to.


### Source


**BBC Science Focus** , August 24, 2026.


### Disclaimer


This article is for **general informational and educational purposes only** . It is not medical advice, a diagnosis or a substitute for consultation with a qualified healthcare professional. Research linking calf muscle pump function with health outcomes does not establish that calf weakness directly causes heart disease or reduced lifespan. If you experience persistent leg swelling, unexplained calf pain, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain or other concerning symptoms, seek appropriate medical attention promptly.
